nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-01.title: Bound and last digit
nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-01.body:
$20^3 = 8000 < 19x83 < 27000 = 30^3$, so the cube root is between $20$ and $30$. A cube ending in $3$ must have a root ending in $7$, so the number is $27^3 = 19683$, and $x = 6$.

**Answer: 6**

nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-02.title: When are the two Tuesdays different?
nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-02.body:
The first Tuesday and the first Tuesday after the first Monday are different days only if the month begins on a Tuesday (then the first Monday is the 7th and the next Tuesday is the 8th). So both months begin on a Tuesday. That means the first month has a number of days divisible by $7$, i.e. exactly $28$ days: it is February (in a non-leap year).

**Answer: February**

nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-02.title: Check the other cases
nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-02.body:
If a month starts on any day other than Tuesday, its first Monday comes before its first Tuesday, so the two named Tuesdays coincide and the travellers could not be in two cities. Hence both consecutive months start on Tuesday; months of $29$, $30$ or $31$ days would shift the weekday by $1$, $2$ or $3$. Only a $28$-day February works.

**Answer: February**

nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-04.title: Complement
nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-04.body:
With $n$ tickets, the chance that all lose is $\frac1{2^n}$; we need $\frac1{2^n} < 0.05$, i.e. $2^n > 20$. Since $2^4 = 16$ and $2^5 = 32$, $n = 5$.

**Answer: 5**

nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-05.title: Monotonicity
nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-05.body:
$2^{2x} - 2^x = 2^x(2^x - 1)$ is increasing where it is positive, so there is at most one solution; $x = 5$ gives $1024 - 32 = 992$.

**Answer: $x = 5$**

nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-06.title: Law of cosines
nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-06.body:
Let $a = x^2+x+1$ (the largest side, since $x > 1$), $b = 2x+1$, $c = x^2-1$. One checks
$$b^2 + c^2 + bc = (4x^2+4x+1) + (x^4 - 2x^2 + 1) + (2x^3 + x^2 - 2x - 1) = x^4 + 2x^3 + 3x^2 + 2x + 1 = a^2.$$
So $a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc\cos A$ with $\cos A = -\frac12$, and $A = 120^\circ$.

**Answer: 120°**

nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-06.title: Try a value
nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-06.body:
Since the answer cannot depend on $x$, try $x = 2$: sides $7, 5, 3$. Then $\cos A = \frac{25 + 9 - 49}{30} = -\frac12$, so $A = 120^\circ$.

**Answer: 120°**

nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-08.title: Rates
nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-08.body:
Let the machines do $p$ and $q$ of the job per hour. Then $5p + 2q = \frac12$ and $\frac32(p+q) = \frac14$, so $p + q = \frac16$. Subtracting $2(p+q) = \frac13$ from the first: $3p = \frac16$, $p = \frac1{18}$, $q = \frac19$. The last quarter takes $\frac14 \div \frac19 = \frac94$ hours.

**Answer: $\frac94$ hours**

nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-08.title: Times for the whole job
nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-08.body:
If the machines need $a$ and $b$ hours alone, $\frac5a + \frac2b = \frac12$ and $\frac3{2a} + \frac3{2b} = \frac14$. Clearing denominators, $10b + 4a = ab = 6a + 6b$, so $a = 2b$. Then $\frac5{2b} + \frac2b = \frac9{2b} = \frac12$, $b = 9$, and a quarter of the job takes $\frac94$ hours.

**Answer: $\frac94$ hours**

nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-09.title: Two cases
nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-09.body:
If $\cos x \ge 0$, $f(x) = 2\cos x$; otherwise $f(x) = 0$. So $f(x) = 1$ means $\cos x = \frac12$, i.e. $x = \frac\pi3$ or $\frac{5\pi}3$ in $[0,2\pi]$: two values.

**Answer: 2**

nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-09.title: Graph
nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-09.body:
The graph of $f$ is $2\cos x$ where cosine is nonnegative and $0$ elsewhere; the line $y = 1$ meets it once on $\left[0,\frac\pi2\right]$ and once on $\left[\frac{3\pi}2, 2\pi\right]$.

**Answer: 2**

nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-10.title: Split 105° as 60° + 45°
nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-10.body:
Angles $B$ and $D$ are right, so $ABCD$ is inscribed in a circle with diameter $AC$. Let $\angle BAC = \alpha$, so $\angle CAD = 105^\circ - \alpha$, $AB = AC\cos\alpha = 2$ and $CD = AC\sin(105^\circ - \alpha) = 2\sqrt2$. Taking $\alpha = 60^\circ$ gives $AC = 4$ from the first and $CD = 4\sin45^\circ = 2\sqrt2$, matching the second; and the ratio $\frac{CD}{AB} = \frac{\sin(105^\circ-\alpha)}{\cos\alpha} = \sin105^\circ + \sin15^\circ\tan\alpha$ is strictly increasing in $\alpha$, so this is the only possibility. Then $BC = 2\sqrt3$, $AD = 2\sqrt2$, and Ptolemy's theorem gives
$$AC\cdot BD = AB\cdot CD + AD\cdot BC = 4\sqrt2 + 4\sqrt6,$$
so $BD = \sqrt2 + \sqrt6$.

**Answer: $\sqrt2+\sqrt6$** (equivalently $2\sqrt{2+\sqrt3}$)

nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-10.title: Extended law of sines
nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-10.body:
In the circle with diameter $AC = 4$, chord $BD$ subtends the inscribed angle $BAD = 105^\circ$, so $BD = AC\sin105^\circ = 4\cdot\frac{\sqrt6+\sqrt2}{4} = \sqrt6 + \sqrt2$.

**Answer: $\sqrt2+\sqrt6$**

nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-11.title: Complement
nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-11.body:
All three white: $\frac5{12}\cdot\frac4{11}\cdot\frac3{10} = \frac1{22}$. So at least one black has probability $1 - \frac1{22} = \frac{21}{22}$.

**Answer: $\frac{21}{22}$**

nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-12.title: Reciprocals add
nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-12.body:
Taking reciprocals, $\frac1{f(x+y)} = \frac1{f(x)} + \frac1{f(y)}$. So $g = \frac1f$ is additive with $g(1) = 1$, hence $g(n) = n$ by induction ($g(n+1) = g(n) + g(1)$). Thus $f(1987) = \frac1{1987}$.

**Answer: $\frac1{1987}$**

nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-13.title: Count after the gifts
nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-13.body:
Each girl received one pencil from each of the $5$ boys, so has $5$. Each boy then also has $5$, and he gave away $12$, so he started with $17$.

**Answer: 17**

nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-13.title: Equation
nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-13.body:
If each boy had $b$, afterwards he has $b - 12$ and each girl has $5$: $b - 12 = 5$, $b = 17$.

**Answer: 17**

nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-14.title: Equilateral triangle
nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-14.body:
The three edges meet at a vertex $V$; $E, F, G$ are each $2$ from $V$ along mutually perpendicular edges. Each side of $EFG$ is $\sqrt{2^2+2^2} = 2\sqrt2$, so the triangle is equilateral with area $\frac{\sqrt3}4\cdot8 = 2\sqrt3$.

**Answer: $2\sqrt3$**

nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-14.title: Coordinates
nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-14.body:
$E = (2,0,0)$, $F = (0,2,0)$, $G = (0,0,2)$. $\vec{EF}\times\vec{EG} = (-2,2,0)\times(-2,0,2) = (4,4,4)$, of length $4\sqrt3$; the area is half: $2\sqrt3$.

**Answer: $2\sqrt3$**

nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-15.title: Quadratic in 4^cos
nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-15.body:
Let $y = 4^{\cos(x/3)} > 0$: $y^2 - y - 2 = (y-2)(y+1) = 0$, so $y = 2$ and $\cos\frac x3 = \frac12$. The smallest positive $\frac x3$ is $\frac\pi3$, so $x = \pi$.

**Answer: $\pi$**

nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-15.title: Check
nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-15.body:
At $x = \pi$: $\cos\frac\pi3 = \frac12$, $16^{1/2} - 4^{1/2} = 4 - 2 = 2$. For $0 < x < \pi$, $\cos\frac x3 > \frac12$, making the left side larger than $2$ (it increases with $y$ for $y > \frac12$).

**Answer: $\pi$**

nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-16.title: Isosceles triangles
nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-16.body:
Since $MN \parallel BC$, $\angle MTB = \angle TBC = \angle MBT$, so triangle $MBT$ is isosceles with $MT = MB = 6$. Likewise $\angle NTC = \angle TCB = \angle NCT$, so $NT = NC = 8$. Hence $MN = MT + TN = 14$.

**Answer: 14**

nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-16.title: Parallel line through the incenter
nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-16.body:
$T$ is the incenter, and the classic fact that the line through the incenter parallel to $BC$ satisfies $MN = MB + NC$ follows from the two isosceles triangles above: $MN = 6 + 8 = 14$.

**Answer: 14**

nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-17.title: Solve for the root
nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-17.body:
Let $y = \sqrt{x/4 - 3} \ge 0$. Then $x/4 + 2 = y^2 + 5$, and squaring $\sqrt{y^2+5} = c + y$ gives $y^2 + 5 = c^2 + 2cy + y^2$, so $y = \frac{5 - c^2}{2c}$. This must be $\ge 0$ (with $c > 0$), so $c \le \sqrt5$. For $c = \sqrt5$, $y = 0$, $x = 12$ works.

**Answer: $\sqrt5$**

nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-17.title: Decreasing function
nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-17.body:
$c = \sqrt{u+2} - \sqrt{u-3} = \frac{5}{\sqrt{u+2}+\sqrt{u-3}}$ with $u = x/4 \ge 3$. This decreases as $u$ grows, so its maximum is at $u = 3$: $c = \sqrt5$.

**Answer: $\sqrt5$**

nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-19.title: Check
nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-19.body:
$3^2 = 9 = 3 + 2\cdot3$. The root $y = -1$ is impossible since $y > 0$, so $x = 2$ is the only solution.

**Answer: $x = 2$**

nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-20.title: Two isosceles triangles
nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-20.body:
Let the bisectors meet at $T$ on $AD$. Since $AD \parallel BC$, $\angle ATB = \angle TBC = \angle ABT$, so $AB = AT$. Similarly $\angle DTC = \angle TCB = \angle DCT$, so $DC = DT$. Since $AB = DC$, $BC = AD = AT + TD = 2AB$, and $AB:BC = 1:2$.

**Answer: $1:2$**

nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-20.title: Work backwards
nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-20.body:
Suppose $AB = 1$ and $BC = 2$. The bisector of angle $B$ meets line $AD$ at the point $T$ with $AT = AB = 1$, i.e. the midpoint of $AD$; by symmetry the bisector of angle $C$ meets $AD$ at the point with $DT = DC = 1$, the same midpoint. In general the two points coincide only when $AB + DC = AD$, i.e. $BC = 2AB$.

**Answer: $1:2$**

nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-21.title: Count edges
nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-21.body:
With $V = 5$, Euler gives $E - F = 3$. Each face has at least $3$ edges and each edge borders $2$ faces, so $2E \ge 3F$, i.e. $2(F+3) \ge 3F$, $F \le 6$. For a lower bound: each vertex has degree at least $3$, so $2E \ge 15$, $E \ge 8$, and $F = E - 3 \ge 5$. A square pyramid has $5$ vertices and $5$ faces.

**Answer: 5**

nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-21.title: Case analysis
nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-21.body:
With only $5$ vertices, faces are triangles or quadrilaterals. All triangles: $E = \frac{3F}{2}$ and $E - F = 3$ give $F = 6$ (two tetrahedra glued on a face). One quadrilateral face: the fifth vertex joins all four of its corners, a square pyramid with $5$ faces. Two quadrilaterals would need at least $6$ vertices. So the minimum is $5$.

**Answer: 5**

nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-23.title: Half an hour per mile
nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-23.body:
A mile of level trail takes $\frac14$ hour each way, $\frac12$ hour for the round trip. A mile that is uphill one way is downhill the other way: $\frac13 + \frac16 = \frac12$ hour for the round trip. So every mile of trail costs $\frac12$ hour over the round trip. In $6$ hours, the trail is $12$ miles long one way, and the round trip is $24$ miles.

**Answer: 24 miles**

nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-23.title: Average speed
nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-23.body:
For each stretch of trail the round-trip average speed is $4$ mph: level ground directly, and up/down with harmonic mean $\frac{2\cdot3\cdot6}{3+6} = 4$. So the whole round trip averages $4$ mph, and $4\cdot6 = 24$ miles.

**Answer: 24 miles**

nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-24.title: Squeeze between squares
nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-24.body:
Let $P = x^2 + 4x + 2$. Then $P^2 = x^4 + 8x^3 + 20x^2 + 16x + 4$, so the expression is $E = P^2 - 4(x-2)$. At $x = 2$, $E = P^2 = 14^2 = 196$.
- If $x \ge 3$: $E < P^2$, and $E - (P-1)^2 = 2P - 1 - 4x + 8 = 2x^2 + 4x + 11 > 0$. So $(P-1)^2 < E < P^2$, not a square.
- If $x \le -7$: $P > 0$ and $E > P^2$, and $(P+1)^2 - E = 2P + 1 + 4x - 8 = 2x^2 + 12x - 3 > 0$ (true for $x \le -7$). So $P^2 < E < (P+1)^2$, not a square.
- For $x = -6, -5, \ldots, 1$ the values of $E$ are $228, 77, 28, 21, 20, 13, 12, 53$; none is a perfect square.

So $x = 2$ is the only integer.

**Answer: 2**

nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-24.title: Check small cases
nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-24.body:
Only finitely many integers escape the squeeze argument. Checking $x = -6, \ldots, 2$ directly, the only perfect square is at $x = 2$: $16 + 64 + 80 + 24 + 12 = 196 = 14^2$.

**Answer: 2**

nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-25.title: Rotate the slices
nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-25.body:
Call the slices $A, B, C$. Round 1: $A_1, B_1$. Round 2: $A_2, C_1$. Round 3: $B_2, C_2$. Three rounds of $30$ seconds: $90$ seconds. Fewer is impossible: there are $6$ sides to toast and only $2$ per round, so at least $3$ rounds.

**Answer: 90**

nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-25.title: Lower bound first
nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-25.body:
$6$ sides, at most $2$ toasted per $30$ seconds, so at least $90$ seconds; the schedule above achieves it.

**Answer: 90**

nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-26.title: Means
nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-26.body:
With $p = \sqrt{1986}$, $q = \sqrt{1988}$: $b = 2\sqrt{pq}$ (twice the geometric mean), $a = p + q$ (twice the arithmetic mean), $c = 2\sqrt{\frac{p^2+q^2}{2}}$ (twice the quadratic mean). For $p \ne q$, GM < AM < QM, so $b < a < c$.

**Answer: $b, a, c$**

nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-27.title: Ordered choices
nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-27.body:
One particular order (G, G, B, B, B) has probability $\frac5{15}\cdot\frac4{14}\cdot\frac{10}{13}\cdot\frac9{12}\cdot\frac8{11} = \frac{40}{1001}$; there are $\binom52 = 10$ orders, giving $\frac{400}{1001}$.

**Answer: $\frac{400}{1001}$**

nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-28.title: Integer conditions
nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-28.body:
$A = 4r^2$ and $B = \frac43r^3$. Then $r = \frac{3B}{A}$ is rational and $4r^2 = (2r)^2$ is an integer, so $k = 2r$ is an integer. Now $B = \frac{k^3}{6}$ must be an integer, so $6 \mid k$; write $k = 6m$. Then $A = 36m^2$ and $B = 36m^3$. $B < 10000$ forces $m^3 < 278$, so $m \le 6$; $A > 1000$ forces $m^2 > 27$, so $m \ge 6$. Hence $m = 6$, $r = 18$ ($A = 1296$, $B = 7776$).

**Answer: 18**

nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-28.title: Check
nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-28.body:
$r = 18$: surface area $4\pi\cdot324 = 1296\pi$, volume $\frac43\pi\cdot5832 = 7776\pi$; both coefficients are between $1000$ and $10000$.

**Answer: 18**

nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-29.title: Telescoping bound
nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-29.body:
For $n \ge 2$, $\frac1{n^2} < \frac1{n(n-1)} = \frac1{n-1} - \frac1n$. So the sum is less than $1 + \left(1 - \frac1{50}\right) < 2$. It is clearly greater than $1$. So the smallest integer larger than it is $2$.

**Answer: 2**

nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-29.title: Known value
nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-29.body:
The full series $\sum \frac1{n^2} = \frac{\pi^2}6 \approx 1.645$, and the partial sum to $50$ is about $1.625$, between $1$ and $2$.

**Answer: 2**

nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-30.title: Angular radii
nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-30.body:
Measure each circle by its angular radius seen from the center $O$ of the sphere: a circle of radius $10$ on a sphere of radius $20$ has angular radius $\theta$ with $20\sin\theta = 10$, so $\theta = 30^\circ$. Tangent circles have centers (on the sphere) at angular distance $60^\circ$, so the unit vectors $u_1, u_2, u_3$ toward the three centers satisfy $u_i\cdot u_j = \frac12$.

By symmetry the fourth circle's center is in the direction of $u_1 + u_2 + u_3$, which has length $\sqrt{3 + 6\cdot\frac12} = \sqrt6$. The angle $\varphi$ to each $u_i$ satisfies $\cos\varphi = \frac{u_1\cdot(u_1+u_2+u_3)}{\sqrt6} = \frac{2}{\sqrt6}$, $\sin\varphi = \frac1{\sqrt3}$. The fourth circle's angular radius is $\varphi - 30^\circ$, so its radius is
$$20\sin(\varphi - 30^\circ) = 20\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt3}\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}2 - \frac{2}{\sqrt6}\cdot\frac12\right) = 10 - \frac{20}{\sqrt6} = 10 - \frac{10\sqrt6}3.$$

**Answer: $10 - \frac{10\sqrt6}{3}$** (equivalently $10 - 10\sqrt{2/3} \approx 1.835$)

nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-30.title: Tetrahedron of cones
nyciml-1986-87-spring-seniora-30.body:
Each circle is cut from the sphere by a plane; the cone from $O$ to a circle of radius $10$ has half-angle $30^\circ$. The three centers on the sphere, $C_1, C_2, C_3$, form an equilateral triangle with $C_iC_j = 2\cdot20\sin30^\circ = 20$, so its circumradius is $\frac{20}{\sqrt3}$ and its plane is at distance $\sqrt{400 - \frac{400}{3}} = \frac{20\sqrt2}{\sqrt3}$ from $O$. The angle $\varphi$ between $OC_i$ and the symmetry axis has $\sin\varphi = \frac{20/\sqrt3}{20} = \frac1{\sqrt3}$. The fourth circle has angular radius $\varphi - 30^\circ$ and radius $20\sin(\varphi - 30^\circ) = 10 - 10\sqrt{\tfrac23}$.

**Answer: $10 - \frac{10\sqrt6}{3}$**
